chunks.text:
# FAQ — What is PiEEG?

PiEEG is a family of EEG shields and boards that turn a Raspberry Pi, Jetson Nano, Arduino, or standalone USB host into a multi-channel brain-computer interface. It measures biosignals including EEG (brain), EMG (muscles), ECG/EKG (heart), and EOG (eyes). The companion PiEEG Server software streams, records, and exposes real-time data over WebSocket, LSL, OSC, and webhooks.
chunks.title: What is PiEEG?

chunks.text:
# FAQ — Who is PiEEG for?

Researchers, students, makers, startups, and educators who want research-grade biosignal acquisition without the cost of traditional lab equipment. If you can run a Python script, you can get started.
chunks.title: Who is PiEEG for?

chunks.text:
# FAQ — What hardware platforms are available?

There are 7 hardware platforms ranging from 8 to 32 channels: PiEEG, PiEEG-16, IronBCI, IronBCI-32, MicroBCI, ardEEG, and JNEEG. See the [Hardware](/hardware) section for full specifications.
chunks.title: What hardware platforms are available?

chunks.text:
# FAQ — Is PiEEG FDA/CE approved for medical use?

<Callout type="error">
  **No.** PiEEG devices are **not** medical devices and have **not** been certified by any government regulatory agency (FDA, CE, or equivalent). They are designed for education, research, and engineering purposes only.
</Callout>

PiEEG must not be used for medical diagnosis, treatment, clinical applications, life-support, or any safety-critical use. See [Liabilities](/hardware/safety/liabilities) and [Safety](/hardware/safety) for full details.
chunks.title: Is PiEEG FDA/CE approved for medical use?

chunks.text:
# FAQ — Is PiEEG safe to use on humans?

When used correctly, yes — but you must follow critical safety rules:

- **Always use battery power** (5 V DC) when measuring biosignals from humans. Never connect a PiEEG device to mains power, USB from a grid-connected computer, or wall outlets while in use with human subjects.
- Do not use if you have a pacemaker or other implanted medical device without consulting a physician first.
- Discontinue use if you experience discomfort or skin irritation.
- There is no patient isolation circuitry on the device, so battery isolation is essential.

You are fully responsible for the safe use of the device.
chunks.title: Is PiEEG safe to use on humans?

The **software and SDKs are MIT licensed** (including PiEEG Server) and fully public on [GitHub](https://github.com/pieeg-club). Hardware designs are proprietary. You can fork, modify, and build freely on the software side.

No. The PiEEG Server includes a browser dashboard for real-time visualization and CSV recording with no code required. For programmatic access, connect any WebSocket client — plain JSON, no SDK required. See the [Quick Start](/software/getting-started/quick-start).

# About PiEEG — About PiEEG

PiEEG is an initiative that makes brain-computer interface (BCI) technology accessible to researchers, students, and makers worldwide. PiEEG provides access to neurobiology through research-grade biosignal hardware compatible with a wide range of electrodes for EEG, EMG, ECG, and EOG — allowing the study and application of neural and biosignal data in real-world conditions.

If you can run a Python script, you can explore the human nervous system.
chunks.title: About PiEEG

chunks.text:
# About PiEEG — What Is PiEEG?

PiEEG is a family of EEG shields and boards that turn a Raspberry Pi, Jetson Nano, Arduino, or standalone USB host into a multi-channel brain-computer interface. The companion **PiEEG Server** software acquires, streams, records, and exposes real-time EEG data over WebSocket, Lab Streaming Layer (LSL), OSC, and webhooks — with a built-in browser dashboard out of the box.

The project spans hardware (from 8 to 32 channels), MIT-licensed software and SDKs, and a global open-source community.

# About PiEEG — Our Mission

For years, the PiEEG team has been dedicated to breaking down the barriers of neuroscience. We believe that measuring the human body's signals — whether from the brain (EEG), muscles (EMG), or eyes (EOG) — should not be restricted to high-cost equipment.

Our mission is to make PiEEG the universal bridge between biology and technology for research purposes. Designed for simplicity and compatible with a vast range of electrodes, PiEEG hardware lets you go from unboxing to data-tracking in minutes.
chunks.title: Our Mission

chunks.text:
# About PiEEG — Our Story

PiEEG is a project born from a shared interest in hardware engineering, signal processing, and neuroscience. The team consists of researchers and engineers who believe that the tools for exploring biosignals should be accessible to everyone.

The project was launched on Crowd Supply, where it raised five times its initial funding goal. Over the years, the team has contributed to the field by publishing findings on Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) and developing open-source software tools. The goal is not just to build devices, but to provide a transparent platform where others can experiment with neural interfaces.

By combining experience in hardware design with machine learning, the team works to ensure PiEEG remains a reliable, entry-level tool for non-medical research and exploration.
chunks.title: Our Story

chunks.text:
# About PiEEG — Core Values

- **Open & Transparent** — Software and SDKs are MIT licensed and fully public. There is no vendor lock-in. The GitHub repositories are the source of truth for every line of software.
- **Community-Driven** — Built by neuroscientists, for neuroscientists. The roadmap is shaped by real user needs.
- **Innovation First** — Pushing the boundaries of what is possible with accessible hardware, from 32-channel EEG to edge AI integration.
- **Quality Matters** — Low cost does not mean low quality. PiEEG uses quality components, rigorous testing, and peer-reviewed validation to deliver research-grade results.

chunks.text:
# Buddy — EEG AI Agent — Buddy — the EEG AI Agent

**Buddy is a 100% browser-based EEG copilot — and it *is* the AI agent.** It pairs a live brain panel with a tool-using LLM that reads your neural state client-side, plus guided pattern training — all powered by Web Bluetooth / Web Serial. There is no server to run, no account to create, and no data leaves the tab.

Buddy is part of [PiEEG Cloud](/cloud). Where the [dashboard](https://cloud.pieeg.com) is for *watching* your signal, Buddy is for *talking to it* — asking questions in plain language, training custom mental-state detectors, and reading an honest, explained picture of your live brain state.

<Cards>
  <Cards.Card title="Open Buddy → buddy.pieeg.com" href="https://buddy.pieeg.com/" />
</Cards>

<Callout type="info">
  Buddy runs entirely in a Chromium browser (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera). The signal pipeline, feature extraction, pattern training, and the AI agent's tool calls all execute client-side — no PiEEG server, no login.
</Callout>
chunks.title: Buddy — the EEG AI Agent

chunks.text:
# Buddy — EEG AI Agent — The brain panel

Buddy reduces the raw stream into language-sized facts and renders them live:

| Card | What it shows |
|------|---------------|
| **State** | Smoothed `focus` / `relax` / `engagement` indices (0–1, within-session), dominant band, and a `warming_up` flag while readings settle. |
| **Band powers** | Relative δ / θ / α / β / γ power, with a per-channel breakdown. |
| **Quality grid** | Per-channel signal status: `good` / `flat` / `rail` / `noisy` / `line`, with RMS and line ratio. |
| **Artifacts** | Discrete transients: blinks, double-blinks, jaw clenches, motion. |
| **Connectivity** | Cross-channel amplitude coupling (Pearson *r* over log band-power envelopes) for a chosen band. |
| **Trends** | Rolling history of state and band power over the session. |
| **Cascade monitor** | Live view of the perception tiers (features → quality → state → events). |
| **Pattern ticker** | Which trained patterns are firing right now, with smoothed probabilities. |
chunks.title: The brain panel

chunks.text:
# Buddy — EEG AI Agent — The AI agent

The chat copilot is a tool-using LLM that runs a multi-turn loop over your live neural cascade — reading state, spectra, artifacts, connectivity, and your trained patterns through read-only tools — and answers in plain language.

It is **100% browser-based**. You bring your own API key, and the agent talks to your chosen provider directly from the tab. There is no PiEEG server hop, and no raw EEG is ever sent to the model.

<Callout type="info">
  This is the browser-native sibling of the server-side [PiEEG Agent](/software/integrations/pieeg-agent). Same idea — talk to your brain signal — but with no Python, no LSL, and no server. See [Browser vs. server-side](#browser-vs-server-side).
</Callout>
chunks.title: The AI agent

chunks.text:
# Buddy — EEG AI Agent — How it works

The agent runs a bounded **tool-calling loop**:

1. Your question is appended to the conversation.
2. The model streams a response; if it requests tools, the agent runs them against the live `BuddyEngine`.
3. Tool results are fed back and the model continues, up to a small iteration cap, until it answers.

The model **pulls** state through tools on demand — it is never streamed raw samples. This solves the rate mismatch between an LLM (~1 Hz of reasoning) and EEG (250–500 Hz of data).
chunks.title: How it works

chunks.text:
# Buddy — EEG AI Agent — Perception cascade (browser edition)

The agent reads a layered reduction of the signal — trimmed to the senses that exist in-browser (no server, no actuators, no notebook/session store):

| Tier | Rate | Representation | Agent sees |
|------|------|----------------|------------|
| T0 Raw | 250 Hz | µV samples | Never |
| T1 Features | ~feature Hz | band powers, quality | Via tools |
| T2 State | ~1 Hz | focus / relax / engagement | Via tools |
| T3 Events | sparse | debounced transitions, artifacts | Via tools |
| T4 Reason | on query | natural-language Q&A + tools | — |

<Callout type="warning">
  The agent **observes and explains — it does not control the device.** Every tool is read-only. If no data is available yet, it says the stream is still warming up rather than guessing.
</Callout>
chunks.title: Perception cascade (browser edition)

chunks.text:
# Buddy — EEG AI Agent — Tools

The agent grounds every claim in a fresh tool call against the live engine:

| Tool | Returns |
|------|---------|
| `get_neural_state` | Smoothed focus / relax / engagement (0–1, within-session), dominant band, quality, `warming_up`. |
| `get_band_powers` | Relative δ / θ / α / β / γ power and per-channel breakdown. |
| `analyze_spectrum` | Individual alpha peak (IAF), aperiodic 1/f slope, theta/beta ratio, spectral entropy, frontal alpha asymmetry (optional single channel). |
| `find_artifacts` | Recent blinks, double-blinks, jaw clenches, motion. |
| `get_recent_events` | Debounced state transitions (focus/relax/engagement/quality high↔low). |
| `get_channel_quality` | Per-channel status (`good`/`flat`/`rail`/`noisy`/`line`), RMS, line ratio. |
| `connectivity` | Cross-channel amplitude coupling (Pearson *r* over log band-power envelopes) for one band. |
| `list_patterns` | Trained pattern detectors with cross-validated balanced accuracy. |
| `detect_patterns` | Which trained patterns are firing now, with smoothed probabilities. |
| `explain_pattern` | Justifies one pattern: threshold, cross-validation, per-channel importance, top features. |
chunks.title: Tools

chunks.text:
# Buddy — EEG AI Agent — Providers

Pick a provider in the Lobby or in **Settings** and paste an API key. Cloud providers stream over their standard APIs; local providers run on your own machine; **Echo** needs no key and is handy for a no-cost demo.

| Provider | Type | Key required |
|----------|------|--------------|
| Anthropic | Cloud | Yes |
| OpenAI | Cloud | Yes |
| Groq | Cloud | Yes |
| Together AI | Cloud | Yes |
| Ollama | Local | No |
| LM Studio | Local | No |
| Echo | Debug | No (built-in) |

<Callout type="info">
  One normalized message/tool shape drives all providers: the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API (OpenAI, Groq, Together, Ollama, LM Studio), the Anthropic Messages API, and the offline Echo provider.
</Callout>
chunks.title: Providers

chunks.text:
# Buddy — EEG AI Agent — Example conversation

```text
you > how's my signal?
buddy > All channels read "good", quality 0.97 — trustworthy.

you > am I focused or relaxed right now?
buddy > Relaxed, for you right now. Alpha is dominant and focus is low.
        (Readings are within-session, not clinical.)

you > which of my trained patterns is firing?
buddy > "meditation" is active (p≈0.88). It's a strong detector —
        leave-one-rep-out balanced accuracy 0.89, reading mostly O1/O2.
```
chunks.title: Example conversation

chunks.text:
# Buddy — EEG AI Agent — Pattern training

Buddy's most powerful sense is a **trained pattern detector** — a custom classifier for any mental state you can reproduce (meditation, focus, imagined movement, etc.).

Training is **contrastive**: you record a `REST` baseline and an `ACTIVE` state across several reps. Buddy then fits a per-pattern detector and scores it honestly:

- **Leave-one-rep-out cross-validation (LORO-CV)** splits by rep, not by sample, so temporal leakage cannot inflate the score.
- **Balanced accuracy** is reported so class imbalance cannot flatter the result.
- **Channel importance** is exposed via spatial (group-lasso) sparsity — you can see which electrodes the detector actually reads.

A trained detector is far more meaningful than the generic `focus` / `relax` indices, and the AI agent can list, detect, and explain your patterns on demand.

<Callout type="warning">
  Buddy is designed for neurofeedback research and UX prototyping — **not clinical use**. All indices are within-session and descriptive, not diagnostic.
</Callout>
chunks.title: Pattern training

chunks.text:
# Buddy — EEG AI Agent — Honest metrics

Buddy is deliberate about what its numbers mean, and its system prompt keeps the agent candid:

- `focus` / `relax` / `engagement` are **0–1 values relative to this session's own range** — described as "high/low for you right now", never absolute or clinical.
- A `warming_up` flag marks the settling period before enough variance is established; the agent says so when a reading is still settling.
- **Pattern scores** are leave-one-rep-out balanced accuracy — honest at the data scale you actually have.
- Poor signal quality or flagged channels are surfaced **before** conclusions are drawn.
chunks.title: Honest metrics

chunks.text:
# Buddy — EEG AI Agent — Privacy

Everything stays in your browser tab:

- Raw EEG is decoded, filtered, and analyzed **client-side** — it is never uploaded to a PiEEG server.
- Trained patterns persist locally in your browser.
- Your API key and every agent request go **directly** from the tab to your chosen LLM provider — there is no PiEEG middleman. The model receives only the **reduced, language-sized facts** returned by tools, never raw EEG. You choose whether to persist the key.
chunks.title: Privacy

# PiEEG Cloud — PiEEG Cloud

**[cloud.pieeg.com](https://cloud.pieeg.com) is the 100% cloud, browser-based PiEEG platform.** Open it in Chrome or Edge and stream in seconds — no Python, no install, no login, no account. Packet decoding, DSP, FFT, spectral analysis, and every experience run entirely client-side in your browser.

<Callout type="info">
  Nothing to set up. Point a Chromium browser at **[cloud.pieeg.com](https://cloud.pieeg.com)**, pick a signal source, and you are streaming. Your EEG never leaves the tab.
</Callout>
chunks.title: PiEEG Cloud

The cloud platform is built from the [PiEEG-server-cloud](https://github.com/pieeg-club/PiEEG-server-plus) project and ships two browser apps plus an optional installable desktop app:

| **[Buddy](/cloud/buddy)** | A browser-native EEG copilot and AI agent: live brain panel, a tool-using LLM that reads your brain state (BYO API key), and guided pattern training. | 100% browser — [buddy.pieeg.com](https://buddy.pieeg.com/) |

<Callout type="info">

</Callout>

# Local Bridge — Local Bridge

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'
chunks.title: Local Bridge

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — Local Bridge

An ultra-fast, secure local gateway that connects the browser-based **Pieeg Cloud** to services on your own network. It receives a real-time data stream from a browser via **WebRTC P2P data channel** and forwards it locally over protocols such as **OSC** — with minimal latency and near-zero setup.

<Callout type="info">
**Direct P2P connection** — all data flows locally (loopback/LAN). Nothing is relayed through the cloud after the initial WebRTC handshake.
</Callout>
chunks.title: Local Bridge

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — Why it exists

Pieeg Cloud runs entirely in the browser and has no backend of its own. To reach local software (VRChat, TouchDesigner, Max/MSP, Ableton via OSC, game engines, etc.), it establishes a **WebRTC peer-to-peer data channel** with the Local Bridge running on your machine. Data flows **directly** between browser and bridge via loopback or LAN — nothing is relayed through the cloud. The bridge turns the incoming JSON stream into real OSC packets on `127.0.0.1` (or any host on your LAN).
chunks.title: Why it exists

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — Features

- **Single standalone binary** — ~5 MB, no runtime, no dependencies to install
- **Instant startup, low memory** — pure Rust / Tokio
- **System tray** — runs quietly in background; right-click to show UI, regenerate code, or quit
- **Direct P2P connection** — WebRTC data channel; all data stays local (loopback/LAN)
- **Reversed pairing flow** — bridge requests a session from the cloud and gets back a 6-character share code; you enter it in Pieeg Cloud
- **Encrypted transport** — DTLS for the P2P data channel; signaling uses HTTPS
- **STUN/TURN aware** — ICE servers provided by the cloud session for reliable NAT traversal
- **Automatic discovery** — finds local OSC apps via mDNS (`_osc._udp`)
- **Protocol-agnostic core** — pluggable adapters; OSC ships first
- **Cross-platform** — Windows, macOS, Linux
chunks.title: Features

chunks.text:

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — Pairing with Pieeg Cloud

1. **Run the Local Bridge**. On startup it contacts the cloud signaling server and displays a 6-character share code (e.g. `KHSP3W`) at `http://127.0.0.1:47800`.

2. In **Pieeg Cloud**, click **Connect to Local Bridge** and enter the share code.

3. The browser and bridge perform a **one-time WebRTC handshake** (SDP/ICE exchange via the cloud signaling server).

4. A **direct P2P data channel** opens between browser and bridge. All data flows **locally** (loopback or LAN) — nothing is relayed through the cloud.

5. Incoming data frames are mapped to OSC and sent to your chosen destination.

<Callout>
**Share code regeneration**: Right-click the system tray icon and select "Regenerate Pairing Code" to create a new cloud session (new code + ICE servers) and disconnect any active session.
</Callout>

The whole setup takes under a minute and requires no technical knowledge.
chunks.title: Pairing with Pieeg Cloud

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — Data Mapping

The router applies two ordered, generic rules — no producer field names are hardcoded:
chunks.title: Data Mapping
1. Explicit Envelope

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — 2. Generic Flatten

Any other JSON object is walked recursively; every number/bool/string leaf becomes an OSC address built from its JSON path. Transport metadata keys (`type`, `t`, `ts`, etc.) are skipped.

**Example:**
```json
{ "channels": [0.1, 0.2, 0.3], "t": 123 }
```

**Becomes:**
```
/pieeg/channels/0  0.1
/pieeg/channels/1  0.2
/pieeg/channels/2  0.3
```

<Callout type="info">
Flattening can be disabled in the UI to forward only explicit `osc` envelopes.
</Callout>
chunks.title: 2. Generic Flatten

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — Configuration

Settings are persisted as JSON and edited from the UI (no manual editing needed):

| OS      | Path                                                              |
| ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Windows | `%APPDATA%\pieeg\LocalBridge\config.json`                        |
| macOS   | `~/Library/Application Support/com.pieeg.LocalBridge/config.json` |
| Linux   | `~/.config/pieeg-local-bridge/config.json`                       |
chunks.title: Configuration

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — CLI Options

| Flag                      | Description                                                     |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--port <PORT>`           | Control-UI port (default `47800`)                              |
| `--signaling-url <URL>`   | Signaling server URL for WebRTC handshake (default `https://pieeg-cloud.fly.dev`) |
| `--connect <SESSION_ID>`  | Connect immediately with this session code and skip the browser |
| `--allow-origin <ORIGIN>` | Add a cross-origin site allowed to call the control API (repeatable) |
| `--no-open`               | Do not open the control UI in a browser on startup             |
chunks.title: CLI Options

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — Architecture

The bridge is deliberately **vendor- and protocol-neutral**:

```
Browser (WebRTC P2P) ──► router (generic mapping) ──► adapters (OSC, …)
```

| Layer     | Role                                                                 |
| --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Transport | Cloud session creation, WebRTC P2P data channel, SDP/ICE handshake via HTTP signaling |
| Currency  | `BridgeMessage { address, args }` — protocol-neutral                 |
| Router    | Generic JSON → `BridgeMessage` mapping (envelope + flatten)          |
| Adapters  | Pluggable `Adapter` trait; OSC/UDP sink with hot-swappable target    |
| Control   | Local HTTP API + embedded UI; pairing code generation; WebRTC signaling endpoint |
| Discovery | Best-effort mDNS `_osc._udp` scan                                    |
| Config    | Persisted, hot-reloadable JSON config; vendor-agnostic CORS origins  |
| Tray      | System tray icon with Show UI / Regenerate Code / Quit menu          |

Adding a new output protocol means adding **one adapter** — nothing else changes.
chunks.title: Architecture

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — Security

- **P2P data channel encrypted with DTLS** — WebRTC data flows directly between browser and bridge (loopback/LAN), not through the cloud
- **One-time signaling handshake** — SDP/ICE exchange uses HTTPS; only occurs at connection setup
- **Share code as secret** — the 6-character code is the trust anchor; regenerate to mint a new cloud session and revoke access
- **CORS agnostic** — no vendor origins baked in; configure allowed origins via `--allow-origin` or JSON config
- **Local-only control API** — listens only on `127.0.0.1`
- **No cloud relay for data** — after handshake, all data stays local
chunks.title: Security

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — System Tray

The bridge runs quietly in your system tray (Windows notification area). Right-click the tray icon for:

- **Show Control UI** — opens `http://127.0.0.1:47800` in your browser
- **Regenerate Pairing Code** — creates a new cloud session (new 6-character code) and disconnects any active session
- **Quit** — stops the bridge cleanly
chunks.title: System Tray

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — Bridge won't start

- Check if port `47800` is already in use: `netstat -an | findstr 47800` (Windows) or `lsof -i :47800` (macOS/Linux)
- Try a different port: `pieeg-local-bridge --port 47801`
chunks.title: Bridge won't start

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — Can't connect from Pieeg Cloud

- Verify the share code is correct (it's case-sensitive)
- Check if your firewall is blocking the connection
- Try regenerating the pairing code from the system tray menu
chunks.title: Can't connect from Pieeg Cloud

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — No OSC output

- Use the mDNS discovery feature in the UI to find local OSC apps
- Verify your OSC application is listening on the configured port
- Check the data mapping rules (enable/disable flattening as needed)
chunks.title: No OSC output

chunks.text:
# Local Bridge — macOS "unidentified developer" warning

- Right-click the app → **Open**, then click **Open** in the dialog
- Or: System Settings → Privacy & Security → allow the app
chunks.title: macOS "unidentified developer" warning

# Cap — Ready-Made Cap

PiEEG recommends the [Nylon EEG Cap](https://pieeg.com/cap-eeg-kit/).  It is made from a comfortable nylon material and comes pre-configured for use with all PiEEG devices.
chunks.title: Ready-Made Cap

chunks.text:
# Cap — DIY Cap

Can use any comfortable caps for you, or create your own cap (DIY cap). Here you can find step-by-step ***[instructions](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/369378602_DIY_-Hat_for_measuring_EEG_with_dry_electrodes_for_PiEEG)*** on how to do that.


All PiEEG devices have a connection Connector Header Through Hole - 2.54 mm, so if you use some other caps, you need to confirm that the connectors have the same view

![Image](/images/hardware/2025/05/app-1-2.png)

To connect the Header in PiEEG devices, which have the following pins

![Image](/images/hardware/2025/05/app-1-1.png)
chunks.title: DIY Cap

chunks.text:
# Cap — Electrode Placement

Whether using dry or wet electrodes, place them according to the international 10-20 system — the standard method for consistent, reproducible EEG electrode positioning across sessions and subjects.

![Image](/images/hardware/2024/08/New-Bitmap-Image-264x300.jpg)
chunks.title: Electrode Placement

chunks.text:
# Cap — Choosing the Right Cap

| Cap Type | Setup Required | Compatibility | Best For |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **PiEEG Nylon Cap** | None | All PiEEG devices | Recommended starting point for most users |
| **Third-Party Cap** | Verify 2.54 mm connector | Must confirm pin pitch | Custom fit, specific channel counts |
| **DIY Cap** | Build from instructions | 2.54 mm pin pitch required | Experimentation, custom layouts, low cost |
chunks.title: Choosing the Right Cap

chunks.text:
# Electrodes — Electrodes

Electrodes are required to measure EEG signals with any PiEEG device. All PiEEG hardware uses a standard 2.54 mm pin pitch connector, making it compatible with a wide range of electrode types.
chunks.title: Electrodes

chunks.text:
# Electrodes — Dry Electrodes

Dry electrodes require no preparation gel or paste, making them ideal for quick setups, everyday use, and longer recording sessions. They are the most convenient option for most users.
Ag/AgCl (Wet) Electrodes
Silver/silver chloride electrodes provide excellent signal quality and are the standard choice in research and clinical settings. They require conductive gel applied to the scalp for optimal contact, but deliver lower impedance and reduced noise compared to dry electrodes.
chunks.title: Dry Electrodes

chunks.text:
# Electrodes — Wet electrodes

Wet electrodes also available directly from the PiEEG Shop. They are fully compatible with all PiEEG devices.
chunks.title: Wet electrodes

chunks.text:
# Electrodes — Choosing the Right Electrode

| Electrode Type | Setup Required | Signal Quality | Best For |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Dry | None | Good | Quick sessions, everyday use |
| Ag/AgCl (Wet) | Conductive gel | Excellent | Research, clinical, high-precision work |

# Power Bank — Power Bank

Power Bank
All PiEEG devices must be powered from a battery (power bank) only — not from mains power. This ensures electrical isolation and safe, clean signal acquisition.
Choosing a Power Bank
For PiEEG, PiEEG-16, and JNEEG, use a power bank with a 5V output, a minimum output current of 3A, and a capacity of no more than 10,000 mAh.
For ardEEG, use a smaller power bank: 5V output with no more than 1A output current and a capacity of up to 1,000 mAh.
A single power bank can supply both the PiEEG device and a connected monitor at the same time, as long as it meets the current requirements for your device.
Choosing a USB Cable
Use the shortest USB cable practical for your setup. Longer cables increase resistance and can cause voltage drops that affect device stability. Always use a thick-gauge cable to ensure sufficient current is delivered to the device.

# How to start. Connections with ardEEG — How to start. Connections with ardEEG

This page explains how to physically connect your ardEEG shield, Arduino UNO R4, and electrodes before starting a recording session.
chunks.title: How to start. Connections with ardEEG

chunks.text:
# How to start. Connections with ardEEG — Step 1 — Attach the ardEEG Shield

Align the ardEEG shield with the header pins on your Arduino UNO R4 and press it firmly into place. Make sure all pins are fully and evenly seated before powering on.
chunks.title: Step 1 — Attach the ardEEG Shield

chunks.text:
# How to start. Connections with ardEEG — Step 2 — Connect the Electrodes

ardEEG uses three types of electrode connections:
- Channel Electrodes (1–8)
- Connect 8 EEG electrodes to channels 1 through 8. Place them on the scalp according to the 10-20 system to capture the EEG signal.
- Reference Electrode: Attach a clip electrode to one ear. This provides a stable voltage reference for all 8 channels.
Bias Electrode: Attach a second clip electrode to the other ear. This actively cancels electromagnetic interference, reducing noise in the signal.
chunks.title: Step 2 — Connect the Electrodes

chunks.text:
# How to start. Connections with ardEEG — Step 3 — Power On

Connect a 5V power bank (max 1A, up to 1,000 mAh) to the Arduino UNO R4. Do not power the device from a PC USB port or mains adapter — battery power only ensures clean signal acquisition. Once powered, proceed to Software Setup to configure the firmware.

![Image](/images/hardware/2025/05/download-3-1-300x181.jpeg)
chunks.title: Step 3 — Power On

chunks.text:
# ardEEG — ardEEG

ardEEG is an open-source shield for the Arduino UNO R4 that measures biosignals — including EEG (electroencephalography), EMG (electromyography), and ECG (electrocardiography).
chunks.title: ardEEG

chunks.text:
# ardEEG — What It Does

ardEEG brings biosignal acquisition to the Arduino platform, making it the most accessible and lowest-cost entry point in the PiEEG device family. It connects directly to the Arduino UNO R4 header and uses the ADS1299 analog front-end chip to capture high-quality biosignal data.
ardEEG is ideal for students, hobbyists, and educators who want to explore EEG, EMG, and ECG measurement without the complexity or cost of a single-board computer setup. It is also well suited for embedded BCI prototypes and low-power standalone applications.
chunks.title: What It Does

chunks.text:
# ardEEG — Key Features:

- Supports EEG, EMG, and ECG measurements
- Connects directly to the Arduino UNO R4 header
- Powered by the ADS1299 analog front-end chip
- Compatible with dry and Ag/AgCl wet electrodes via 2.54 mm pin pitch connectors
- Low power — runs from a small 5V power bank (up to 1,000 mAh, max 1A)
chunks.title: Key Features:

chunks.text:

| Feature | PiEEG | ardEEG |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Host board** | Raspberry Pi 4 / 5 | Arduino UNO R4 |
| **Channels** | 8 | 8 |
| **Power requirement** | 3A, up to 10,000 mAh | Max 1A, up to 1,000 mAh |
| **Operating system** | Raspberry Pi OS (Linux) | Arduino firmware |
| **Best for** | Research, full BCI setup | Education, prototyping, embedded |


![ardEEG Arduino low-cost device to measure EEG, EMG, EKG](/images/hardware/2024/05/genereal-300x112.jpg)

# How to start. Software with ardEEG — How to start. Software with ardEEG

ardEEG uses a two-part setup: an Arduino sketch that reads and transmits biosignal data over Wi-Fi, and a Python script on your computer that receives and visualises it in real time.
All scripts are available on [GitHub](https://github.com/Ildaron/ardEEG/).
chunks.title: How to start. Software with ardEEG
Step 1 — Upload the Arduino Sketch

chunks.text:
# How to start. Software with ardEEG — Step 2 — Run the Python Script

On your computer, run the Python visualisation script. It connects to the Arduino over Wi-Fi and displays the incoming biosignal data as a real-time graph with a band-pass filter applied.  
Make sure your computer is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as the Arduino before running the script.
chunks.title: Step 2 — Run the Python Script

chunks.text:
# How to start. Software with ardEEG — Step 3 — Verify the Signal

Once both scripts are running, you should see a live graph of the EEG, EMG, or ECG signal. If no data appears, check that:

The Arduino is powered on and connected to Wi-Fi
Your computer is on the same network
The correct Wi-Fi credentials were entered before uploading the sketch

# Aura VR Intro — Aura VR

**Aura VR** is an open-source hardware shield and wearable bio-signal interface designed by PiEEG. It captures real-time biometric and motion data streams—including EMG, EEG, and ECG—and sends them directly into VR, AR, and PC applications.

![Image](/images/hardware/2026/01/Aura_VR.png)


---
chunks.title: Aura VR

chunks.text:
# Aura VR Intro — Key Features

- **Motion Tracking & Movement Control:** Features an onboard **LSM6DS3TR-C** 6-axis IMU with an integrated 3D gyroscope and accelerometer, enabling direct motion and head-tracking controls inside virtual environments.
- **Muscle-Based Interactions:** Captures real-time EMG muscle signals, allowing you to trigger extra skills, gestures, or action inputs in VR without pressing physical buttons, as well as track athletic effort in sports performance applications.
- **Orientation Precision:** Select hardware revisions include an **LIS3MDL** 3-axis magnetometer for enhanced rotational orientation accuracy. *(Note: Check your specific hardware version for magnetometer inclusion.)*
- **Electrode Compatibility:** Connects to both dry and Ag/AgCl wet electrodes via standard 2.54 mm pin-pitch headers.

---
chunks.title: Key Features

chunks.text:
# Aura VR Intro — Where to Find Aura VR

* **GitHub Repository:** Access open-source schematics, hardware files, and calibration scripts at [github.com/Ildar2021/Aura_VR](https://github.com/Ildar2021/Aura_VR).
* **Official Website:** Find hardware documentation and project updates at [pieeg.com](https://www.pieeg.com).
* **Video Demos:** Watch setup guides and live EMG/IMU demos on the [PiEEG YouTube Channel](https://www.youtube.com/@pieeg/videos)

# Specification — Mask Details. Electrodes Location. 10 flat dry silver-silver chloride (Ag/AgCl) electrodes are specialized biosignal sensors used for recording surface biopotentials, ECG/EMG monitoring, and EEG research without requiring messy conductive gels The LSM6DS3TR-C from STMicroelectronics is a 6-axis Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) combining a 3-axis digital accelerometer and a 3-axis digital gyroscope The LIS3MDL is an ultra-low-power, high-performance digital 3-axis magnetic sensor made by STMicroelectronics (not in all version).
Bracelet - Material Nylon, Rubber ![Image](/images/hardware/2026/01/Aura_VR_Elec_Loc.png)
chunks.title: Mask Details. Electrodes Location.

chunks.text:
# Specification — Hardware Architecture

*   **Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC):** Dual **ADS1299** (supporting up to 16 (depends of version) simultaneous channels of high-resolution biopotential data).
*   **Microcontroller (MCU):** **STM32WB** series (Dual-core ARM Cortex-M4/M0+ for robust application processing and dedicated wireless stacks).
*   **Wireless Connectivity:** **Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE 5)** for low-latency, ultra-low-power data transmission.
chunks.title: Hardware Architecture

chunks.text:
# Specification — Signal Integrity & Electrodes

*   **Ultra-Low Noise:** **1.0 µVₚₚ** (Peak-to-Peak Noise), ensuring clean signal baselines even in challenging environments.
*   **Electrode Compatibility:** Supports both **Gel** (wet) and **Dry** electrode systems for flexible deployment.
chunks.title: Signal Integrity & Electrodes

# IronBCI — IronBCI

IronBCI documentation for device setup, wireless software, and video instructions.

<Cards>
	<Cards.Card title="Version 1.2" href="/hardware/devices/ironbci/version-1-2" />

</Cards>


IronBCI is a low-cost, wearable Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) brain-computer interface with 8 channels for measuring EEG, EMG, ECG, and EOG biosignals. Unlike the PiEEG shield family, IronBCI is a fully standalone device — no Raspberry Pi or single-board computer required.
chunks.title: IronBCI

chunks.text:
# IronBCI — What It Does

IronBCI connects wirelessly to a laptop, smartphone, or tablet over BLE, streaming 8 channels of biosignal data at 250 samples per second. It is powered by a small LiPo battery, making it compact and portable for wearable and mobile BCI applications.
IronBCI includes a mobile SDK, making it suitable for building iOS and Android BCI applications as well as desktop integrations.
chunks.title: What It Does

chunks.text:
# IronBCI — Key Features:

- 8 channels of simultaneous biosignal acquisition
- Supports EEG, EMG, ECG, and EOG measurements
- Wireless BLE connection — no cables to a host computer
- Streams at 250 samples per second
- Compatible with dry and Ag/AgCl wet electrodes via 2.54 mm pin pitch connectors
- Powered by a LiPo battery (200 mAh recommended, 2.0 mm JST connector)
- Includes a mobile SDK for iOS and Android development, Python SDK and software PiEEG-server
chunks.title: Key Features:

chunks.text:
# IronBCI — How It Differs from PiEEG

| Feature | PiEEG | IronBCI |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Host required** | Raspberry Pi 4 / 5 | **None** — standalone |
| **Connectivity** | Wired (GPIO) | **Wireless** (BLE) |
| **Channels** | 8 | 8 |
| **Power source** | Power bank (5V, 3A) | LiPo battery (200 mAh) |
| **Mobile SDK** | No | **Yes** |
| **Best for** | Desktop research, fixed setup | Wearable, mobile, on-the-go BCI |
chunks.title: How It Differs from PiEEG

# How Connect Cables — How Connect Cables

IronBCI-32 uses 34 electrode connections in total:
- 32 channel electrodes — placed on the scalp to measure biosignals
- 1 Reference electrode — clip electrode attached to one ear
- 1 Bias electrode — clip electrode attached to the other ear

All electrodes use a 2.54 mm pin pitch connector. Refer to the connection schematic above for the exact pin position of each electrode on the board headers.
chunks.title: How Connect Cables

chunks.text:
# How Connect Cables — Step 1 — Connect the Channel Electrodes

Connect the 32 channel electrodes to the numbered header pins on the IronBCI-32 board, following the schematic. Use wet (Ag/AgCl) electrodes for best signal quality.
Place the electrodes on the scalp according to the international 10-20 system for consistent and reproducible electrode positioning. For a 32-channel setup, electrodes typically cover the full scalp including frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital regions.
chunks.title: Step 1 — Connect the Channel Electrodes

chunks.text:
# How Connect Cables — Step 2 — Connect the Reference Electrode

Attach a clip electrode to one ear. This provides a stable voltage reference for all 32 channels. Connect its cable to the REF pin on the board.
chunks.title: Step 2 — Connect the Reference Electrode

chunks.text:
# How Connect Cables — Step 3 — Connect the Bias Electrode

Attach a second clip electrode to the other ear. This actively drives a common-mode signal back into the body to cancel electromagnetic interference. Connect its cable to the BIAS pin on the board.
chunks.title: Step 3 — Connect the Bias Electrode

chunks.text:

# IronBCI-32 — IronBCI-32

IronBCI-32 documentation for startup, cable connections, and software workflows.

<Cards>
	<Cards.Card title="How to Start" href="/hardware/devices/ironbci-32/how-to-start" />
	<Cards.Card title="Cable Connections" href="/hardware/devices/ironbci-32/cable-connections" />
	<Cards.Card title="Software" href="/hardware/devices/ironbci-32/software" />
</Cards>





IronBCI-32 is a high-channel-count, brain-computer interface with 32 simultaneous channels for measuring EEG, EMG, ECG, and EOG biosignals. It connects to a laptop or desktop over USB serial, delivering a full 32-channel data stream compatible with the BrainFlow SDK and the PiEEG Server.
chunks.title: IronBCI-32

chunks.text:
# IronBCI-32 — What It Does

IronBCI-32 is the highest channel count device in the PiEEG family, making it well suited for high-density EEG research, advanced neural decoding, and applications that require full-scalp coverage. It transmits data over a USB serial connection using the FreeEEG frame format, which is natively supported by BrainFlow.
To ensure clean signal acquisition, IronBCI-32 requires galvanic isolation between the device and the host computer. The laptop receiving data must run on battery power only — disconnected from mains — to eliminate 50/60 Hz line noise and prevent ground loop interference.
chunks.title: What It Does

chunks.text:
# IronBCI-32 — Key Features

- 32 channels of simultaneous biosignal acquisition
- Supports EEG, EMG, ECG, and EOG measurements
- USB serial connection to laptop or desktop
- Compatible with BrainFlow SDK out of the box
- Compatible with wet electrodes via 2.54 mm pin pitch connectors
- Powered by 5V USB battery — mains power strictly not permitted
- Supported by PiEEG Server for streaming and integrations
chunks.title: Key Features

chunks.text:
# IronBCI-32 — How It Differs

Depending on your research needs, choose the model that fits your host environment and channel density requirements.

| Feature | PiEEG | IronBCI | IronBCI-32 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Host board** | Raspberry Pi | **None** (standalone) | Laptop / desktop |
| **Channels** | 8 | 8 | **32** |
| **Connectivity** | Wired (GPIO) | **Wireless** (BLE) | USB serial |
| **BrainFlow support** | No | No | **Yes** |
| **Best for** | General research | Wearable / mobile | High-density EEG |

---

Safety: IronBCI-32 must be powered from a 5V battery only. It must never be connected to mains power via USB or any other means. See the Liabilities page before use.
chunks.title: How It Differs

# JNEEG — JNEEG

JNEEG is a shield for the NVIDIA Jetson Nano that measures biosignals — including EEG (electroencephalography), EMG (electromyography), and ECG (electrocardiography) — across 8 simultaneous channels.
What It Does
JNEEG brings the PiEEG biosignal acquisition experience to the NVIDIA Jetson Nano platform. It connects directly to the Jetson Nano GPIO header and uses the ADS1299 analog front-end chip to capture 8 channels of high-quality biosignal data in real time.
Because it runs on the Jetson Nano, JNEEG is particularly well suited for applications that benefit from on-device GPU acceleration — such as real-time machine learning inference on EEG data, neural decoding pipelines, and computer vision combined with BCI input.

Key Features:
- 8 channels of simultaneous biosignal acquisition
- Supports EEG, EMG, and ECG measurements
- Connects directly to the NVIDIA Jetson Nano GPIO header
- Powered by the ADS1299 analog front-end chip
- Compatible with dry and Ag/AgCl wet electrodes via 2.54 mm pin pitch connectors
- On-device GPU acceleration available via Jetson Nano


![JNEEG Jetson Nano Nvidia low-cost device to measure EEG, EMG, EKG](/images/hardware/2024/05/JNEEG-300x300.jpg)
chunks.title: JNEEG

# What need equipment except JNEEG — Required Equipment

To start measuring Bio Data with PiEEG, it is necessary to have the following parts:

- Power Bank: A 5V power bank with a minimum output current of 3A and a capacity of no more than 10,000 mAh. See the Power Bank page for full requirements and recommendations.

- Peripherals: A USB keyboard and USB mouse to interact with the Raspberry Pi desktop.

- Display: A portable monitor or screen. Power it directly from the power bank using a USB cable.

-  Jetson Nano: Jetson Nano (with mciroSD card, connection to power bank)

- EEG cap: A cap to hold the electrodes in position on the scalp. See the Cap page for options including the recommended PiEEG nylon cap and DIY instructions.

- Electrodes: 8 EEG electrodes (dry or Ag/AgCl wet) with cables, plus 2 clip electrodes for the reference and bias connections. See the Electrodes page for compatible types.

chunks.text:
# How to start. Software with JNEEG — PiEEG Server

JNEEG runs the official [PiEEG Server](https://github.com/pieeg-club/PiEEG-server) —
the same real-time streaming, dashboard, recording, and integrations available on
the Raspberry Pi boards. It is an 8-channel board (single ADS1299); run it with
`--device jneeg`, which applies the `jetson-nano` hardware profile automatically
(600 kHz SPI, GPIO on `/dev/gpiochip0`).

<Steps>
chunks.title: PiEEG Server

chunks.text:
# How to start. Software with JNEEG — Enable SPI on the 40-pin header

SPI is off by default on the Nano. Enable it with NVIDIA's config tool:

```bash
sudo /opt/nvidia/jetson-io/jetson-io.py
```

In the menu: **Configure 40-pin header** → enable **spi1** → **Save and reboot**.
After reboot, confirm the device node exists:

```bash
ls /dev/spidev0.0
```
chunks.title: Enable SPI on the 40-pin header

chunks.text:
# How to start. Software with JNEEG — Grant SPI/GPIO access

Add your user to the `spi` and `gpio` groups so you don't need `sudo`:

```bash
sudo groupadd -f spi
sudo usermod -aG spi,gpio "$USER"
```

Log out and back in (or reboot) for the groups to take effect.
chunks.title: Grant SPI/GPIO access

chunks.text:
# How to start. Software with JNEEG — Install the server

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install pieeg-server[rpi]
```

<Callout type="info">
  The `rpi` extra just installs `spidev`, which is generic Linux SPI and works on
  the Jetson Nano. The Pi-only `setup.sh` script is not used on Jetson.
</Callout>
chunks.title: Install the server

chunks.text:
# How to start. Software with JNEEG — Verify and run

```bash
pieeg-server doctor          # diagnose SPI, GPIO, and dependencies
pieeg-server --device jneeg  # start streaming (8 channels)
```

The `jetson-nano` profile auto-detects from `/proc/device-tree/model`. Open
**http://localhost:1617** for the dashboard.

</Steps>

<Callout type="warning">
  **DRDY pin check (one-time).** The `jetson-nano` profile assumes the data-ready
  line (header pin 7) maps to line offset **216** on `/dev/gpiochip0`. If samples
  never arrive, confirm the offset for your JetPack release with
  `sudo apt install -y gpiod && gpioinfo gpiochip0`, then pass the chip explicitly:
  `pieeg-server --device jneeg --gpio-chip /dev/gpiochip0`.
</Callout>
chunks.title: Verify and run

To save Raw data to Excel, you can use the following [script](https://github.com/pieeg-club/EEG-with-JetsonNano/blob/master/GUI/2.Save_data.py) for Jetson Nano.

chunks.text:
# Octopus 16 — What It Does

Octopus 16 brings high-density biosignal acquisition to microcontrollers  the Seeed Studio  ESP32-S3, enabling portable, wireless, and low-cost 16-channel EEG data acquisition. It utilizes Texas Instruments analog front-end chips (such as the ADS131M08) to capture high-quality 24-bit biosignal data.

Octopus 16 is ideal for researchers, students, and developers building advanced BCI prototypes, wireless neural-interface applications, and multi-channel embedded BCI setups.
chunks.title: What It Does

chunks.text:
# Octopus 16 — Key Features:

- **16-Channel Support:** Measures up to 16 channels of EEG, EMG, or ECG data simultaneously.
- **24-bit ADC Resolution:** Powered by high-precision ADS131M08 analog front-end chips.
- **Wireless & Portable Firmware:** Supports firmware written for Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32 S3 with Bluetooth streaming options.
- **Developer Tools:** Includes Python-based data processing scripts (FFT, signal visualization) and GUI visualization tools (`SDK_Data_Visual.py`).
- **Low Power:** Suitable for wearable, battery-powered BCI applications.

chunks.text:
# Octopus 16 — Pogo Pin Care & Maintenance

> [!IMPORTANT]  
> **Important Notice: Pogo Pin Care & Maintenance**  
> The Octopus 16 utilizes high-precision spring-loaded pogo pins to ensure reliable electrical contact. Over time and under heavy usage, individual pogo pins may become stuck, compressed, or jammed inside their housing.

---
chunks.title: Pogo Pin Care & Maintenance

chunks.text:
# Octopus 16 — 🔍 Why Do Pogo Pins Get Stuck?

Pogo pins rely on an internal spring mechanism. A pin becomes stuck (impacted) primarily due to external environmental factors:

* **Dirt, Dust, and Debris:** Fine particles, dust, and hair inside the pin housing can block the internal spring.
* **Liquid Contaminants:** Oils, moisture, or sticky substances entering the pin barrel cause the internal mechanism to seize.
* **Side-Angle Pressure or Excess Force:** Applying lateral pressure during insertion or over-compressing the pins can cause mechanical binding.

---
chunks.title: 🔍 Why Do Pogo Pins Get Stuck?

chunks.text:
# Octopus 16 — ⚠️ Important Disclaimer & Policy

* **User Responsibility:** Contamination, dirt accumulation, and mechanical wear resulting from improper handling or environmental exposure are **not covered under warranty**.
* **Continued Usage:** If one or more pins become stuck or impacted, the Octopus 16 can often still function, provided the stuck pins maintain adequate contact with the skin for data transmission.

---
chunks.title: ⚠️ Important Disclaimer & Policy

chunks.text:
# Octopus 16 — 🛠️ Best Practices to Prevent and Fix Stuck Pins

To maintain optimal performance and prevent pins from sticking:
chunks.title: 🛠️ Best Practices to Prevent and Fix Stuck Pins

chunks.text:
# Octopus 16 — 1. Keep the Pins Clean

* **Periodically clean** the pin tips with an Isopropyl Alcohol (IPA > 90%) swab or brush to prevent sticky buildup.
* **Use compressed air** to blow out loose dust or debris from around the pin bases.
chunks.title: 1. Keep the Pins Clean

chunks.text:
# Octopus 16 — 2. Handle with Care

* **Insert and align** the device straight down vertically ($90^\circ$ angle). Avoid pushing or tilting the pins sideways while under pressure.
* **Do not force or over-compress** the header beyond its intended travel limit.
chunks.title: 2. Handle with Care

chunks.text:
# Octopus 16 — 3. How to Unstick an Impacted Pin

1. **Apply IPA:** Place a drop of high-purity Isopropyl Alcohol (IPA) directly into the affected pin's barrel to dissolve internal grime or sticky residues.
2. **Exercise the Plunger:** Lightly tap or exercise the plunger gently with a non-metallic tool to help the internal spring push back up. 
3. **Dry Thoroughly:** Allow the IPA to fully dry before powering on the device.

> [!WARNING]  
> **Do not use oil-based lubricants or grease**, as they attract more dirt and permanently damage electrical conductivity.
chunks.title: 3. How to Unstick an Impacted Pin

chunks.text:
# PiEEG-8 — What It Does

PiEEG-8 turns a Raspberry Pi into a full brain-computer interface. It connects directly to the Raspberry Pi GPIO header and uses the ADS1299 analog front-end chip to acquire up to 8 channels of high-quality biosignal data in real time.  
Captured data is streamed, recorded, and processed by the PiEEG Server software, which exposes it over WebSocket, LSL, OSC, and webhooks — and includes a built-in browser dashboard out of the box.
chunks.title: What It Does

chunks.text:
# PiEEG-8 — Key Features

* **8 channels** of simultaneous biosignal acquisition
* Supports **EEG, EMG, and ECG** measurements
* Connects directly to the **Raspberry Pi GPIO header**
* Compatible with **dry and Ag/AgCl wet electrodes** via 2.54 mm pin pitch connectors
* Works with the **PiEEG Server** for real-time streaming, recording, and integrations
* Fully **open-source** hardware and software

![PiEEG low-cost device to measure EEG, EMG, EKG](/images/hardware/2024/05/pieeg-300x238.png)
chunks.title: Key Features

chunks.text:
# What equipment is needed except PiEEG-8 — Required Equipment

To start measuring Bio Data with PiEEG-8, it is necessary to have the following parts:

- Power Bank: A 5V power bank with a minimum output current of 3A and a capacity of no more than 10,000 mAh. See the Power Bank page for full requirements and recommendations.

- Peripherals: A USB keyboard and USB mouse to interact with the Raspberry Pi desktop.

- Display: A portable monitor or screen. Power it directly from the power bank using a USB cable.

- Raspberry Pi: RasberryPi4,5(with mciroSD card, connection to power bank)

- EEG cap: A cap to hold the electrodes in position on the scalp. See the Cap page for options including the recommended PiEEG-8 nylon cap and DIY instructions.

- Electrodes: 8 EEG electrodes (dry or Ag/AgCl wet) with cables, plus 2 clip electrodes for the reference and bias connections. See the Electrodes page for compatible types.

![Image](/images/hardware/2025/05/app-1-300x286.png)

# How to start. Software with PiEEG-8 — Software with BrainFlow library for PiEEG-8

PiEEG-8 was added to [Brainflow](https://brainflow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/SupportedBoards.html) library

To create such board, you need to specify the following board ID and fields of BrainFlowInputParams object:

- BoardIds.PLAYBACK_FILE_BOARD

- master_board, it should contain board ID of the device used to create playback files

- file, it should contain full path to recorded file

- optional: file_aux, use it if your master board has auxiliary preset

- optional: file_anc, use it if your master board has ancillary preset

This page explains how to physically connect your PiEEG-16 shield, Raspberry Pi, and electrodes before starting a recording session.
chunks.title: How to start. Connections with PiEEG-16

chunks.text:
# How to start. Connections with PiEEG-16 — Step 1 — Attach the PiEEG-16 Shield

Align the PiEEG shield with the 40-pin GPIO header on your Raspberry Pi and press it firmly into place. Make sure all pins are seated correctly before powering on.
chunks.title: Step 1 — Attach the PiEEG-16 Shield

chunks.text:
# How to start. Connections with PiEEG-16 — Step 2 — Connect the Electrodes

PiEEG-16 uses three types of electrode connections:  
- Channel Electrodes (1–8)  
  Connect 16 EEG electrodes to channels 1 through 16. These are placed on the scalp according to the 10-20 system and capture the EEG signal.  
- Reference Electrode  
  Attach a clip electrode to one ear. This provides a stable voltage reference for all 8 channels.  
- Bias Electrode  
  Attach a second clip electrode to the other ear. This actively cancels electromagnetic interference from the signal, reducing noise.  

Refer to the connection diagram image above for the exact pin positions of each electrode on the PiEEG connector header.
chunks.title: Step 2 — Connect the Electrodes

chunks.text:
# How to start. Connections with PiEEG-16 — Step 3 — Power On

Connect your power bank to the Raspberry Pi. Once booted, proceed to Software Setup to install and launch PiEEG Server.  

![Image](/images/hardware/2024/08/Img4-2-300x138.png)  

A full PDF quick start manual with connection diagrams is available on [GitHub](https://github.com/pieeg-club/PiEEG-16/blob/main/PiEEG_quick_start.pdf) with SDK launch

chunks.text:
# PiEEG-16 — PiEEG-16

PiEEG-16 is the expanded version of the original PiEEG shield, doubling the channel count from 8 to 16. It connects directly to the Raspberry Pi GPIO header and uses two ADS1299 analog front-end chips in daisy-chain configuration to deliver 16 channels of high-quality biosignal data in real time.  
This makes PiEEG-16 well suited for full-coverage EEG recordings, higher-density EMG setups, and research applications that require more electrode positions than the 8-channel PiEEG can provide.  
Captured data is streamed, recorded, and processed by the PiEEG Server software, which exposes it over WebSocket, LSL, OSC, and webhooks — with a built-in browser dashboard included.  

Key Features:
- 16 channels of simultaneous biosignal acquisition
- Supports EEG, EMG, and ECG measurements
- Connects directly to the Raspberry Pi GPIO header
- Dual ADS1299 analog front-end chips in daisy-chain configuration
- Compatible with dry and Ag/AgCl wet electrodes via 2.54 mm pin pitch connectors
- Works with the PiEEG Server for real-time streaming, recording, and integrations

chunks.title: EEG During Activity (Noise Guide)

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Recording EEG During Activity

The PiEEG XR mask is designed to be worn under a headset while you move. Movement is also the most demanding condition for EEG: the brain signal is only tens of microvolts, while activity produces artifacts that can be hundreds of times larger. This page explains **why the signal gets noisy during activity**, **how to set up the mask**, and — most importantly — **how to confirm the signal is real before you start recording.**
 
<Callout type="info">
  This guide is specific to the **XR mask** (dry electrodes, worn under a headset, during movement). For the general lab setup with clip electrodes and a wired board, see the [Noise Elimination Guide](/hardware/signal-quality/noise-elimination/).
</Callout>
chunks.title: Recording EEG During Activity

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Reasons — why the signal gets noisy during activity

EEG amplitude sits in the range of roughly **10–100 µV**. Nearly every source of movement noise is larger than that, so the goal is to control these sources rather than filter them out afterwards.
 
**Motion artifact (electrode–skin movement).** The main problem during any activity. Each electrode forms a small chemical voltage with your skin; when it slides or lifts even slightly, that voltage jumps — producing swings from tens of µV up to the millivolt range that bury the EEG. Dry electrodes are more prone to this than gel, because the contact is less stable.
 
**Muscle activity (EMG).** Movement makes the jaw, forehead, neck, and scalp muscles fire. EMG is broadband (roughly 20 Hz up past 300 Hz), so it contaminates the higher EEG bands directly and, at high amplitude, bleeds into the lower bands too.
 
**Cable movement.** A cable that swings and flexes as you move generates charge through friction and also acts as an antenna for mains and Wi-Fi interference. A cable running from the head to a laptop is a common, avoidable noise source.
 
**Sweat and skin changes.** Activity changes skin impedance as you sweat. This shows up as slow baseline drift (below ~1 Hz), and if sweat bridges two electrodes, as sudden shifts.
 
**Body rhythm (footfall and pulse).** Each step and heartbeat moves the head slightly, adding a rhythmic low-frequency artifact that rises with your level of effort.
 
<Callout type="warning">
  Most "the data is too noisy during activity" cases are **motion + cable + sweat**, not a hardware fault. Confirm the board itself is clean first using Test 1 in the [Noise Elimination Guide](/hardware/signal-quality/noise-elimination/), then apply the recommendations below.
</Callout>
chunks.title: Reasons — why the signal gets noisy during activity

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Recommendations — how to keep the signal clean

Good preparation is what separates usable data from noise. Do this every session.
 
<Steps>
chunks.title: Recommendations — how to keep the signal clean

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Clean and prep the skin

Wipe the electrode contact areas with an alcohol pad to remove oil, sweat residue, and makeup, then let the skin dry. Clean skin lowers impedance and helps dry electrodes hold a stable contact while you move.
chunks.title: Clean and prep the skin

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Fit the mask firmly and evenly

Use your headset's **original mask together with the silicone insert**, and adjust it until it sits firmly with no gaps or bending. Every electrode needs steady, even pressure — a mask that shifts under the headset is the fastest way to lose the signal.
chunks.title: Fit the mask firmly and evenly

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Optionally. Assist dry electrodes with a little gel

The XR mask supports both **dry and gel** electrodes. Adding a small amount of conductive gel or saline to the dry contacts stabilizes the electrode–skin interface and is the single most effective way to cut motion artifact during activity.
chunks.title: Optionally. Assist dry electrodes with a little gel

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Remove the cable from the equation

The XR streams over **Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE 5)**. Streaming wirelessly to the headset or phone eliminates cable-sway and interference entirely. If you must stay wired, clip the cable to your shirt with a strain-relief loop near the head so it can't swing or tug on the mask.
chunks.title: Remove the cable from the equation

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Stabilize reference, bias, and ground

Confirm the reference and bias/ground contacts are solid and won't shift. An unstable reference makes the whole trace drift or rail — it looks like massive noise but is really one bad contact.
 
</Steps>
chunks.title: Stabilize reference, bias, and ground

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Before you start — confirm the signal is real

**Do not begin recording until you have confirmed live brain data is coming through.** Starting on a dead or railed channel wastes the whole session. Work through the three checks below in order — they take under a minute and tell you the difference between real EEG and random noise.
 
<Steps>
chunks.title: Before you start — confirm the signal is real

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Confirm data is streaming

Open your app (BodyPress or your own client) and look at the live traces before anything else:
 
- The device is **connected** (BLE paired, or cable seated) and the app shows a **live, scrolling** signal.
- **Every channel is moving.** A channel that is a perfectly flat straight line is **not connected** — that electrode has no skin contact.
- The **sample counter is advancing** with no large gaps. Frequent dropped packets mean a weak BLE link — move the receiver closer.
- **Let the band-pass filter settle.** For the first few seconds after start the trace swings widely while the filter adjusts; wait until it calms before judging anything.
chunks.title: Confirm data is streaming

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Read the live baseline

With the mask on and sitting still, each channel should be a **relatively flat line that gently wanders within a few µV to a few tens of µV.** Compare what you see against this table:
 
| What you see | What it means | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gentle line, small wander, reacts to blinks | **Good** — real signal | Ready to test below |
| Flat straight line, no movement | Dead channel / no contact | Reseat that electrode, add gel (Optionally) |
| Pinned at the top or bottom (railed) | Saturated — usually a bad **reference** | Re-check reference / bias / ground |
| Thick constant fuzzy band | **50/60 Hz mains hum** | Battery power only, move from EMI, apply notch |
| Large slow rolling wander | Drift (sweat, motion, filter settling) | Wait to settle, dry skin, steady the mask |
| All channels identical | Reference / common-mode problem | Fix the reference contact |
chunks.title: Read the live baseline

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Run the functional tests

These prove the signal is **coming from you**, not from the environment. Do each one while watching the live trace:
 
| Test | What to do | What you should see | Confirms |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Blink test** | Blink hard 3–5 times | Large, sharp deflections — strongest in the **front (forehead) channels** | Frontal electrodes have good contact and are picking up real biosignal |
| **Eye movement** | Look left, then right | Slower deflections, opposite direction on left vs right frontal channels | Frontal contact and correct channel mapping |
| **Jaw clench** | Clench your teeth briefly | A burst of **high-frequency fuzz** (EMG) that stops when you relax | Electrodes are responsive; also shows what muscle noise looks like |
| **Alpha test** | Only for Academic Version. Sit still, relax, **close eyes ~10 s**, then open | A rise in smooth **8–12 Hz (alpha)** waves in the **back (occipital) channels** while eyes are closed, dropping when you open them | This is the definitive proof you are recording real brain activity |
 
<Callout type="warning">
  **The blink test is your one-second sanity check — always do it.** If blinking produces no visible deflection on the frontal channels, those electrodes are not making contact. Stop and fix the fit (reseat, add gel(Optionally), tighten the mask) before going any further. There is no point recording a channel that can't even see a blink.
</Callout>
chunks.title: Run the functional tests

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Take a still baseline

Once blinks are clearly visible and the alpha test works, record **20–30 seconds standing still**. This clean reference lets you compare the moving data against a known-good stretch later.
 
</Steps>
chunks.title: Take a still baseline

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — During the session

- Warm up before recording the "real" data, so sweat and contact have stabilized.
- Keep the jaw and forehead relaxed where the activity allows — clenching adds strong EMG.
- Note the timestamps of large movements so you can correlate them with spikes later.
- If the trace suddenly rails, reseat the mask — it's usually a shifted electrode or a loose reference, fixable mid-session.
chunks.title: During the session

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Cleaning the signal in software

Even with a good setup, moving data benefits from processing:
 
- **Band-pass filter** (about **1–40 Hz**) to cut low-frequency sweat/footfall drift and most high-frequency EMG.
- **Notch filter** at **50 Hz or 60 Hz** (match your region) to remove mains hum.
- **Artifact / epoch rejection** to drop the windows around large movements instead of trying to save them.
- **ICA** to separate and remove muscle and cable components when you need the higher bands.
<Callout type="info">
  Filtering cannot recover a channel that was fully saturated by motion — it only cleans data that still contains real signal. Getting the fit and contact right is always worth more than post-processing.
</Callout>
chunks.title: Cleaning the signal in software

chunks.text:
# EEG During Activity (Noise Guide) — Quick checklist

- [ ] Board noise floor verified clean (Test 1 in the Noise Elimination Guide)
- [ ] Skin wiped with alcohol and dried
- [ ] Mask firm and even under the headset, no shifting
- [ ] Optionally, A little gel/saline on dry electrodes
- [ ] Streaming over BLE, or cable clipped with a strain-relief loop
- [ ] Reference / bias / ground contacts solid
- [ ] **Data streaming, every channel moving (none flat or railed)**
- [ ] **Blink test visible on frontal channels**
- [ ] **Alpha rises with eyes closed**
- [ ] Still baseline recorded
- [ ] Band-pass + notch applied, large-movement epochs rejected
chunks.title: Quick checklist

# Step 1 — Replace the Face Mask — Step 1 — Replace the Face Mask

---
How to connect PiEEG XR
---

The PiEEG XR has two physical parts that attach to your headset:

1. A **silicone face mask** with built-in electrodes. This replaces (or sits in place of) your headset's original facial interface and touches your face to pick up EEG/EMG signals.
2. A **BCI enclosure (box)** connected to the mask by a cable. Inside the box is the brain-computer interface, which streams data wirelessly over **BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy)**.

To set up, you swap in the mask, mount the box on the headset, and power it from a USB-C power bank. Once powered, the device starts advertising over Bluetooth under the name **`PiEEG XR`**.

> [!NOTE]
> Example shown is for the **Meta Quest 3**. The enclosure and mask are configured per headset model — see the [Required Equipment](#) page for compatibility.

General view of the device:

![PiEEG XR — rear view](/images/hardware/2026/01/pieeg_XR_back.png)

---
chunks.title: Step 1 — Replace the Face Mask

chunks.text:
# Step 1 — Replace the Face Mask — Step 1 — Replace the Face Mask

Remove the original facial interface from your headset and snap the PiEEG XR mask into place. It attaches with four buckles.

1. Remove the original facial interface.
2. Align the four buckles on the interface.
3. Press down to snap the **two back** buckles.
4. Press down to snap the **two front** buckles.

![Replacing the PiEEG XR face mask](/images/hardware/2026/01/pieeg_xr1.jpg) 

> [!TIP]
> If you'd rather keep your existing mask, you can instead remove just the **silicone insert** from the PiEEG XR and fit it into your own setup.

---
chunks.title: Step 1 — Replace the Face Mask

chunks.text:
# Step 1 — Replace the Face Mask — Step 2 — Mount the BCI Enclosure

The BCI box mounts to the headset using the head strap. The best fit is achieved by removing the strap, seating the box, and reattaching the strap over it.

1. Remove the head strap from the VR headset.
2. Place the plastic BCI box against the headset, then reattach the head strap to hold it in place.
3. Route the cable from the mask to the box. The device is now mounted.

![Mounting the PiEEG XR BCI enclosure](/images/hardware/2026/01/PiEEG_XR_11.png)

---
chunks.title: Step 2 — Mount the BCI Enclosure

chunks.text:
# Step 1 — Replace the Face Mask — Step 3 — Power On

Connect a **5 V USB-C power bank** to the PiEEG XR.

Once powered, the device begins advertising over Bluetooth as **`PiEEG XR`**. You can now pair it and start streaming — see the [PiEEG Software page](#) for connecting and recording.

chunks.text:
# FAQ — The device is not visible

This is usually a power supply problem.

- Use a **USB-to-USB** cable (USB on one end, USB on the other). This is the most reliable option.
- To connect to a battery, you can use a **USB to USB-C adapter** on the other end.
- Open the case from the box and check whether an **LED lights up inside** when you connect power. If no LED comes on, check your cable.

See [Required Equipment](https://docs.pieeg.com/hardware/devices/PiEEG_XR/required-equipment/) for the recommended power setup.
chunks.title: The device is not visible

chunks.text:
# FAQ — The silicone mask fell off

Use your headset's **original mask together with our silicone insert**, and adjust it manually until it sits firmly in place with no gaps or bending.

More detail on [How to Connect PiEEG XR](https://docs.pieeg.com/hardware/devices/PiEEG_XR/connections/).
chunks.title: The silicone mask fell off

chunks.text:
# FAQ — I can't connect to the data

This is usually a **BLE** issue — the fix is to update the microcontroller firmware.

See [Service → Update Framework](https://docs.pieeg.com/hardware/devices/PiEEG_XR/Service/) for step-by-step instructions.
chunks.title: I can't connect to the data

Poor contact or environmental noise is the most common cause.

See [Poor Signal / Noise](#) and the [Noise Elimination Guide](https://docs.pieeg.com/hardware/signal-quality/noise-elimination/).

chunks.text: # PiEEG XR Intro — PiEEG XR Intro PiEEG XR is a Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) platform designed to bridge consumer-grade EEG hardware with WebXR-based Extended Reality (XR) environments. It enables real-time, neural-adaptive avatar behavior and interactions directly within a browser stack, without requiring proprietary SDKs or native application containers. By decoding continuous electroencephalography (EEG) signals into affective and cognitive states, PiEEG XR brings a user's internal neural correlates — such as attention, relaxation, and focus — into virtual environments like the Meta Quest browser or social VR platforms via **OSC**. > This section covers the **hardware** and **how to get started**. For software setup and usage, see the [PiEEG Software page](#).
chunks.title: PiEEG XR Intro

# What equipment is needed besides PiEEG — Power

The PiEEG XR is powered by a **5 V power bank** connected over a **USB-C cable**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Use only USB-C supplies rated for power delivery. For the most reliable connection, we recommend a **USB-C to USB-A cable**.

![PiEEG XR USB-C connection](/images/hardware/2026/01/PiEEG_XR_USB_C.bmp)
chunks.title: Power

chunks.text:
# What equipment is needed besides PiEEG — Headset

We recommend a **headset with a built-in battery**, so it can also supply power to the PiEEG XR.

![PiEEG XR headset](/images/hardware/2026/01/PiEEG_XR_Headset.bmp)
chunks.title: Headset

chunks.text:
# What equipment is needed besides PiEEG — Compatibility

The PiEEG XR works with **Meta Quest**, **Meta Quest 3**, **PICO**, and other headset models.  

> [!IMPORTANT]  
> The device housing and mask are configured for the specific headset model they were made for. For example, a unit built for the **Meta Quest 3** fits **only** the Meta Quest 3.   

If you want to adapt the setup for a different headset or mask, a **DIY kit** manual is coming soon. It will let you customize the configuration for any device and mask.
chunks.title: Compatibility

# Service — Update Framework

If you have trouble connecting to the software over **BLE**, the fix is usually to update the microcontroller firmware by uploading a new **hex file**.
chunks.title: Update Framework

chunks.text:
# Service — What You Need

- An **ST-Link** programmer
- The cables included in the package with the ST-Link
- A computer with a free USB port

> [!NOTE]
> The ST-Link and its cables ship inside the same package.

![ST-Link programmer](/images/hardware/2026/01/PiEEG_XR_15.jpg)
chunks.title: What You Need

chunks.text:
# Service — Step 1 — Connect the ST-Link

Connect the ST-Link to your computer over USB. It should appear as a **COM port** in Device Manager.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> If the ST-Link is not recognized, update its **driver** and reconnect.
chunks.title: Step 1 — Connect the ST-Link

chunks.text:
# Service — Step 2 — Install STM32CubeProgrammer

Download and install **STM32CubeProgrammer** — the official STMicroelectronics tool for flashing firmware:

[st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubeprog.html](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubeprog.html)
chunks.title: Step 2 — Install STM32CubeProgrammer

chunks.text:
# Service — Step 3 — Wire the Device (SWD)

Connect the ST-Link to the **ironbci** board using the four cables, over the **SWD** interface.

| ST-Link | ironbci | Signal |
|---------|---------|--------|
| GND | GND | Ground reference |
| RST | RST | Reset (NRST) |
| SWD | SWD | Data line (SWDIO) |
| CLK | CLK | Clock line (SWCLK) |

![SWD wiring between ST-Link and ironbci](/images/hardware/2026/01/PiEEG_XR_13.png)    
STL link connection   
![images](/images/hardware/2026/01/PiEEG_XR_14.jpg)
chunks.title: Step 3 — Wire the Device (SWD)

chunks.text:
# Service — Step 4 — Flash the Firmware

1. In **STM32CubeProgrammer**, click **Connect**.
2. Open the new **hex file**.
3. Upload it to the device.
4. **Disconnect** the device and **reset** it.

Get the latest hex file here:

[PiEEG_XR_Hardware / Firmware / hex](https://github.com/pieeg-club/PiEEG_XR_Hardware/tree/main/Firmware/hex)
chunks.title: Step 4 — Flash the Firmware

chunks.text:
# Service — Video Guide

<Cards>
  <Cards.Card title="Video: Update the firmware step by step" href="https://youtu.be/zU82j_DZxko" />
</Cards>
chunks.title: Video Guide

chunks.text:
# Service — 2. Noise

Check the connection between the electrodes and the skin — it should be firm and consistent.  
To eliminate noise, follow the standard recommendations that apply to all PiEEG setups:  

[Noise Elimination Guide →](https://docs.pieeg.com/hardware/signal-quality/noise-elimination/)
chunks.title: 2. Noise

chunks.text:
# Service — 3. Mask Doesn't Sit Correctly

If the mask has shifted or fallen out of position, reseat the soft part so it sits correctly.

> [!TIP]
> A stable, well-positioned mask is the single biggest factor in clean signal quality.

*   **Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC):** Dual **ADS1299** (supporting up to 16 (depends of version) simultaneous channels of high-resolution biopotential data).
*   **Microcontroller (MCU):** **STM32WB** series (Dual-core ARM Cortex-M4/M0+ for robust application processing and dedicated wireless stacks).
*   **Wireless Connectivity:** **Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE 5)** for low-latency, ultra-low-power data transmission.

*   **Ultra-Low Noise:** **1.0 µVₚₚ** (Peak-to-Peak Noise), ensuring clean signal baselines even in challenging environments.
*   **Electrode Compatibility:** Supports both **Gel** (wet) and **Dry** electrode systems for flexible deployment.

# Signal Quality — Signal Quality
